5: Female thread unions and connectors are fluid-path components with two or three female threaded ports.
6: Female thread unions and connectors are fluid-path components with two or three female threaded ports. Compatible male fittings and sealing assemblies connect flexible or rigid tubing to join, split or combine lines. Bulkhead versions also secure the connection to an instrument panel.
7: The FOREACH range includes U standard unions, US square-body unions, PMU bulkhead unions, UT tees and UY Y connectors. This guide covers M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF ports and 0.5–2.0 mm bores. Available dimensions and materials differ by series.
8: In this range, a union primarily joins fluid lines. Each currently listed website model uses the same thread at all its fluid ports, with M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF options across the range. Different-thread adapters require a specific model and supply arrangement. A straight, same-thread connection is generally called a union; a conversion between different interfaces is an adapter. Branch and panel-mounted versions are described as tees, Y connectors and bulkhead unions.
9: How do female thread unions connect flexible and rigid tubing?
10: First terminate the tubing with a suitable male fitting, then install it in the female body. Rigid tubing usually needs a nut and ferrule, compression-ring or flanged assembly matched to its outside diameter and port geometry. Flexible tubing can use a compatible threaded hose barb. The complete assembly must both retain the tubing and seal the port.
11: U standard union section from the fitting catalogue, with an enlarged central bore
12: Figure 1 | Female ports and central passage of a U standard union. This is a body section; tubing also requires compatible male fittings and seals. Source: English fitting catalogue, page 82.
13: For a matching flat-bottom port and tubing assembly, the thread supplies axial clamping force while the seal forms through correct contact between the sealing component, tube end and port seat. Identical threads alone do not ensure a seal if the seat geometry, port depth or fitting projection differs.
14: The female body receives a male termination; the tubing must be terminated before installation. Unscrewing a termination and pulling tubing off a barb are separate service operations. Stop and depressurize the system first, then inspect the seals and tube ends. Match replacement parts to the original assembly: similar-looking components may use different sealing structures.

19: How do U, US, PMU, UT and UY connectors differ?
20: Choose the number of passages and mounting method first. U and US join two lines; PMU adds bulkhead mounting; UT and UY provide three interconnected ports for splitting or combining flow. The square US body differs from the standard U shape, but appearance does not establish bore size or pressure capability.

The allowable pressure of the complete connection depends on the body, seals, tubing and operating temperature.

44: How should M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF ports and seals be matched?
45: M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF are different threads and must not be screwed together. M6×1 has a 6 mm nominal diameter and 1 mm pitch; 1/4-28 UNF has a 1/4-inch nominal diameter and 28 threads per inch. Similar diameters do not establish compatibility. Forcing a mismatch can damage plastic threads or tilt the fitting.
46: Record the connection thread, sealing structure and tubing dimensions separately for each port.
51: Complete thread specification, male/female form and mating port; M6×1 and 1/4-28 UNF are parallel threads
52: M6 or 1/4 alone can omit the pitch or standard; force cannot correct a mismatch
54: Flat-bottom or other seat, port depth, fitting nose length and specified sealing assembly
55: A tightened thread does not prove the sealing component is correctly seated
57: Tube ID, OD and material; the specified ferrule, compression-ring or flanged assembly
58: OD selects the retaining/sealing components; ID affects passage alignment
60: Record every port's specification and matching components
61: Checking one port does not establish that all ports are compatible
62: Both ends of U-M6-20-PP-N are M6×1; both ends of U-U28-20-PP-N are 1/4-28 UNF. Each currently listed U, US, UT, UY or PMU website model uses the same thread at all fluid ports, but tubing and terminations still need separate selection. For different-thread ends, provide both thread specifications, tubing dimensions and fluid to FOREACH to establish the model, availability and mating components.
63: Body markings help identify ports: M indicates M6×1 and E indicates 1/4-28 UNF. Confirm against the full model and port documentation. Flat-bottom assemblies seal through correct contact between the sealing components and port seat. If the face seal leaks, inspect tube seating, sealing components and the port. Use thread tape or other auxiliary sealing materials only when the assembly instructions specify them.
64: How does bore size relate to tubing size and retained volume?
65: Bore size describes the internal fluid passage; thread size describes the mechanical port interface. They are separate parameters. US-M6 models, for example, share M6×1 ports but offer 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mm bores. Changing the bore may leave the mating thread unchanged while changing the transition to the tube ID.
66: US square-body union outline and section; A indicates bore diameter and dimensions are in millimeters
67: Figure 3 | A denotes the internal bore of the US union. US-M6 options are 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 mm; A is neither thread diameter nor tube OD. Source: English fitting catalogue, page 82.
68: Start with tube ID and target flow, then check whether the fitting becomes a local restriction. Under comparable conditions, a smaller passage may increase pressure drop, while a larger cavity may increase the volume that must be flushed. Passage length, bends, termination geometry, viscosity and operating flow also matter. Bore size alone cannot guarantee flow or carryover performance.
69: Matching the tube ID to the fitting bore and seating the tube correctly helps reduce steps and stagnant spaces at the connection. These are important conditions for low-retention assemblies. System carryover also depends on internal volume, insufficiently flushed areas and operating sequence, so evaluate it with an actual displacement test.
70: For reagent switching, sample transfer and wash circuits, test flushing after installation. Use the actual tube lengths, connectors and operating flow, and a permissible tracer or concentration measurement to record the flushing volume needed to restore the outlet to its target condition. Assess this together with leaks, pressure drop and bubbles when deciding whether the bore suits the fluid path.
71: How are female threaded tees and Y connectors used to split or combine flow?
72: UT and UY have three interconnected ports, so either can split one stream into two or merge two streams. A tee suits a straight main line with a side branch; a Y connector provides angled branches. Check tubing direction, bend clearance and mounting-hole positions before comparing bore sizes and operating conditions.
73: UT tee and UY Y-connector passages, with enlarged intersections and through-bore labels
74: Figure 4 | UT tee above and UY Y connector below, with enlarged passage intersections on the right. Both support splitting or merging; actual direction and branch flow depend on the system. Source: English fitting catalogue, page 83.
75: A passive three-port connector does not regulate the flow split. Even equal tube diameters can produce different flows when lengths, downstream backpressures, valve openings or local resistances differ. Equal delivery needs suitable flow control or metering, verified with both branches operating and with each branch operating alone.
76: Combining streams does not establish complete mixing. Homogeneity also depends on flow ratio, fluid properties and the downstream passage. Neither a T nor a Y shape guarantees it. When one branch is idle, check for backflow caused by pressure in another branch; use appropriate valves or other isolation measures where required.
77: UT and UY mounting holes allow the branch node to be supported so tubing weight does not continuously load the ports. Leave tool access for tightening, removal and cleaning. Any T-versus-Y pressure-drop comparison must use the actual flow, passage geometry and fluid properties.
78: How is a PMU bulkhead union mounted, and which thread serves which function?
79: PMU-M12-U28-20-PP-N separates mounting from fluid connection. Its external M12×1.5 thread receives the mounting nut; the two female fluid ports are 1/4-28 UNF and the bore is 2.0 mm. M12 in the model does not describe the fluid ports.
80: PMU assembly showing panel, nut, female threaded body and tubing terminations on both sides
81: Figure 5 | PMU bulkhead union assembly: the panel is clamped between the nut and body shoulder. This model requires a matching nut and permits panel thickness up to 12.5 mm. Source: English fitting catalogue, page 83.
82: This PMU model accepts a panel no thicker than 12.5 mm and requires a matching nut. Confirm orientation, cutout and clamped thickness before securing the panel between the shoulder and nut. The 12.5 mm value is panel thickness, not hole diameter or insertion depth of a fluid fitting.
83: Before assembly, verify the full PMU model, matching nut and panel drawing. Inspect threads, shoulder and cutout edges; remove burrs and debris.
84: Pass the body through the panel and secure it with the matching nut. Hold the body against rotation so connected tubing is not twisted.
85: Fit each side with a termination compatible with the 1/4-28 UNF port and sealing seat. Treat panel clamping and fluid sealing as separate tightening requirements.
86: Provide clearance on both sides for terminations, nut tools and tubing bends, with suitable tube supports.
87: Check sealing and flow at the intended temperature, pressure and flow rate. Add an air-ingress check under vacuum for suction-side use.
88: Choose PMU for nut-secured bulkhead mounting; U standard unions join tubing directly. Other unions with retaining-ring mounts follow their own panel and ring limits, separately from the PMU limit of 12.5 mm.

102: How should leaks, air ingress or reduced flow be diagnosed?
103: Stop and release residual pressure before locating the fault at a port, tubing termination or body. Do not repeatedly tighten an unverified assembly: mismatched components, an unseated tube, damaged seals and cracked ports require different remedies.
104: Work through the symptoms and retest under actual operating conditions after repair.

126: For first assembly, verify the complete body, termination and tubing combination. For maintenance, also inspect seal deformation, wear and tube-end damage. A reusable body does not automatically make seals or preassembled components reusable. Tightening torque and allowable pressure depend on materials, seal design and operating temperature; values from another fitting do not transfer directly.
128: Can these unions convert M6 to 1/4-28 UNF?
129: Each currently listed U, US, UT, UY and PMU website model has matching fluid-port threads, so these models do not directly convert M6×1 to 1/4-28 UNF. U-M6-20-PP-N has two M6×1 ends; U-U28-20-PP-N has two 1/4-28 UNF ends. For conversion, provide both threads, tubing dimensions and fluid so FOREACH can confirm the specific model and mating components.
130: Should a leaking female threaded connection be taped or tightened further?
131: Stop and depressurize first. Check tube seating, sealing components and the port seat. In a flat-bottom face-sealing assembly, thread tape cannot repair a leaking face seal and further tightening may damage the plastic body. Correct the mating parts or replace damaged components, then tighten and leak-test according to the assembly instructions.
